title: A Lament over Moab
summary: The oracle against Moab begins with sudden disaster: two of its chief cities are destroyed in a single night. Mourning spreads town by town across the land, people shave their heads and put on sackcloth, and refugees flee south carrying what they can. Remarkably, the prophet's own heart cries out for Moab, even as he announces that worse is still to come.
story: The oracles against the nations moved from Babylon and Assyria (chapters 13 and 14) to Philistia on Judah's western border (14:28-32). Now they cross to Moab on the east, across the Dead Sea. Chapters 15 and 16 form a single oracle, the longest against any of Judah's small neighbors. Moab was a near relative and an old rival, and the oracle's surprising tone of grief shows that God's judgment on the nations is not a matter for Judah to gloat over. Chapter 16 will continue the lament and raise the question of whether Moab might find refuge in Zion.
historical:
Moab occupied the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, roughly between the Arnon gorge in the north and the Zered brook in the south, with rich grazing and farmland in the tableland north of the Arnon that it contested with Israel for centuries. Genesis traces the Moabites to Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 19:37), and Ruth, the great-grandmother of David, was a Moabite. Relations were often hostile. Around 840 BC King Mesha of Moab threw off the rule of Israel's house of Omri (2 Kings 3), and his victory inscription, the Mesha Stele, discovered at Dhiban (biblical Dibon) in 1868, names several towns in this chapter, including Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Jahaz, and Horonaim. In Isaiah's time Moab, like Judah, paid tribute to Assyria.

The disaster described here cannot be tied with certainty to a known event. Suggestions include one of the Assyrian campaigns in the region in the late eighth century BC, raids by desert tribes from the east, or an earlier attack in the century before Isaiah whose oracle the prophet takes up and reapplies (16:13 calls it a message spoken earlier). The flight of refugees southward toward Zoar suggests an invader from the north. Jeremiah 48, a century later, reuses many lines of Isaiah 15 and 16 for a new judgment on Moab in the Babylonian period, which shows that later prophets treated this oracle as a word that could speak again. Moab faded as an independent people after the Babylonian era.
cultural:
The chapter is a catalogue of ancient mourning customs. People shaved their heads and cut off their beards, put on sackcloth (a coarse cloth of goat or camel hair worn against the skin), and wailed in the streets, the public squares, and on the flat rooftops where families spent much of their time. Israel knew the same customs, though the law restricted some of them (Deuteronomy 14:1). The temple and high places at Dibon (verse 2) were Moabite shrines, most likely to Chemosh, Moab's national god, who is named on the Mesha Stele and in 1 Kings 11:7. Going up to weep at them shows the people turning to their own gods in the crisis.

The place names trace a map of the disaster. Ar and Kir were major cities, Kir probably the fortress capital also called Kir-hareseth (modern Kerak). Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Nebo, and Medeba lay on the northern tableland. Zoar lay at the south end of the Dead Sea. The Brook of the Willows is probably a stream on Moab's southern border. Dimon in verse 9 is likely a wordplay on Dibon, echoing the Hebrew word for blood, dam.
literary: Isaiah 15 is a lament in poetry, the kind of dirge sung over a fallen city. It is built almost entirely of place names and verbs of grief: wail, weep, cry out, lament. The effect is cumulative, as if the reader moves through the country hearing mourning from each town in turn. The double line of verse 1, “destroyed in a night”, gives the shock of the news. The most arresting line is verse 5, “My heart cries out over Moab”, in which the speaker (the prophet, or God through him) joins the mourners rather than standing apart. The chapter ends not with comfort but with a further threat, a lion upon the fugitives, leaving the lament open into chapter 16.

outline.t: Ar and Kir destroyed in a night
Mourning in the towns: shaved heads, sackcloth, and wailing
The prophet's grief and the flight of the refugees
The outcry fills Moab, and more trouble is coming

doctrines.note: God's judgment reaches Moab as it reached Judah. The chapter does not state Moab's sin (chapter 16 names its pride); it concentrates on the human cost of the disaster.
The chapter lingers over grief without hurrying past it. The prophet names town after town and the losses of ordinary people, treating a foreign people's suffering as worth mourning.
Moab goes up to its temple and high places to weep, but its gods cannot reverse the disaster. Chapter 16:12 will make the point explicit.

words.note: Zaaq, to cry out, a loud cry of distress or appeal for help. It is the word used for Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 2:23). In verses 4 and 5 it describes both Moab's cities and the prophet's own heart, so that the prophet takes up the same cry as the victims.
Yalal, to wail or howl. It is a key word of the oracles against the nations and appears twice here. It names the high, loud keening of public mourning, not quiet sorrow.
Saq, sackcloth, rough cloth made from goat hair, used for grain sacks and worn as a sign of grief or repentance. English sack comes from the same Semitic word by way of Greek and Latin.

Bamah, a high place, a raised shrine or platform for worship, often on a hill. The Bible repeatedly condemns high places in Israel as sites of idolatry. Here the Moabites turn to their own high places in grief.

christ: This chapter contains no prediction of the Messiah, and its link to Christ is thematic. The prophet's heart crying out for an enemy people anticipates the compassion Jesus showed when he wept over Jerusalem, a city that was about to reject him and face destruction (Luke 19:41-44). It also fits the Bible's steady refusal to let God's people treat judgment on others as entertainment. Moab's own story in Scripture includes Ruth, a Moabite woman who became part of the line of David and so of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). A people under judgment in Isaiah 15 had already contributed to the family through whom the Messiah came.

hard.q: Why would a prophet of Israel grieve over Moab, Israel's enemy?
hard.a: Readers have puzzled over the tenderness of verse 5 and 16:9-11. Some think the speaker is the prophet himself, moved by the scale of suffering even among enemies. Others think the voice is God's, and see here a picture of a judge who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (compare Ezekiel 18:23). A few scholars read the lament as ironic or conventional, a formal dirge that need not express personal feeling, since mourning songs over enemies could also be mocking. The sustained detail and the repetition in chapter 16 make most readers take the grief as genuine. On that reading, the oracle shows that judgment can be just and still grievous, and that God's people are to feel it rather than cheer it.

questions: Isaiah mourns for Moab, a rival nation. How do you respond when disaster falls on people you consider opponents?
The Moabites go up to their high places to weep. Where do people turn when their world collapses, and what do those places offer or fail to offer?
What does it teach about God that a prophet announcing his judgment can also say, my heart cries out?
